meta.romanizationConvention: Tergar liturgy style: ཟ→Z, ཞ→ZH, བྱ→J. Approximate Lhasa reading, not phonetic; no tone or vowel length marked.
meta.idIsStable: The 'id' field is a permanent key. Store review progress against it; re-importing a newer export must not lose progress.

cardGuidance.answerSide: ALWAYS show the romanization when the answer is revealed. There is no test left to protect at that point, and the pronunciation is part of what is being learned.
cardGuidance.promptSide: On discrimination cards, hide the romanization only for groups where hideRomanizationOnPrompt is true — those are groups whose members are told apart by their romanization, so showing it lets the learner bypass the script. Where all members share one romanization it is safe, and useful, to show.
cardGuidance.distractorCap: Some groups are large. Cap wrong answers at three or four, chosen at random from the group, rather than offering every member.
cardGuidance.otherCardTypes: For plain recall and cloze there is no reason to hide the romanization anywhere.

entries.notes: Two different words share this spelling: the plural marker (སེམས་ཅན་འདི་དག་ “these sentient beings”) and the verb stem དག་ “to be pure” (དག་པར་གྱུར་ “becomes purified”). Both are DAK, as is བདག་ “I” — three DAKs to keep apart.

entries.notes: All five forms mean the same thing; the choice depends on the suffix of the preceding syllable — after ད་བ་ས་ → ཀྱི་; after ག་ང་ → གི་; after ན་མ་ར་ལ་ → གྱི་; no suffix or after འ་ → འི་ or ཡི་. You only need to recognise them, not memorise the rules. Class mnemonic: ghee is sticky, so it is connective.

entries.notes: Do not confuse this noun with the identically spelled ablative particle ལས་ “from / than”. entries.notes: Traditionally one of the seven ལ་དོན་ particles. For location it comes directly after the place; for possession directly after the possessor. entries.notes: Primary use: marks the agent actively performing a volitional action, usually near the start of the sentence; normally left untranslated. Form depends on the preceding suffix — after ད་བ་ས་ → ཀྱིས་; after ག་ང་ → གིས་; after ན་མ་ར་ལ་ → གྱིས་; no suffix or after འ་ → ས་ or ཡིས་. Secondary use: after a non-sentient thing it is instrumental — “through / with / by means of”. Both can appear in one sentence, one marking the agent and one the instrument. Class mnemonic: geese are always active, so they are agentive.

entries.notes: Bound form — does not stand alone. It appears as ཆེན་པོ་ “great” (and the comparative ཆེ་བ་), and inside compounds: ཐུགས་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོ་ “great compassion”, བཏང་སྙོམས་ཆེན་པོ་ “great equanimity”. Its look-alike ཅན་ is a SUFFIX meaning “endowed with”, not a verb — it never means anything on its own either. IMPORTANT PAIR: exactly homophonous with སྩོལ་ “to bestow, grant” (SYL-005) — opposite directions of giving and seeking, distinguished only in writing. entries.notes: Forms abstract nouns (སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ emptiness, ཆོས་ཉིད་ dharmatā) and adds emphasis to a noun or pronoun (སངས་རྒྱས་ཉིད་ “buddhahood itself”, རང་ཉིད་ “oneself”). Renders Sanskrit -tā / -tva.

example.english: I dedicate, so that they may strive for the state of buddhahood itself.

entries.notes: Adjective མྱུར་བ་ + ལ་དོན་ དུ་ forming an adverb — the standard Tibetan way of making adverbs of manner. The subjoined ྱ is silent in Lhasa reading: MYUR is read NYUR.

example.english: By this virtue may I swiftly

entries.notes: Literally “hand-seal” (ཕྱག་ hand, honorific + རྒྱ་ seal). Both a ritual hand gesture and, by extension, an authenticating seal — hence Mahāmudrā, the “Great Seal”. entries.notes: The central Kagyü meditative system. Named a “seal” because all phenomena are stamped with the nature of mind. Tibetan script reconstructed from the printed phonetics — the Chariot PDF uses a legacy Tergar font whose script does not extract.
sources: Kagyü Ngöndro (Chariot for Traveling the Noble Path)

IMPORTANT PAIR: homophonous with the imperative particle ཅིག་ (NEC-074) and with the ཅིག་ of གྱུར་ཅིག — same sound CHIK, entirely different function. Tibetan script reconstructed from the printed phonetics — the Chariot PDF uses a legacy Tergar font whose script does not extract.

example.english: not omitting even a single being,

entries.notes: Concessive / additive particle. After གཅིག་ it gives “even one”; after a verb it gives “although”. Alternates as ཡང་ and འང་ by preceding final, exactly like the ཀྱི་ / གི་ / གྱི་ series. Tibetan script reconstructed from the printed phonetics — the Chariot PDF uses a legacy Tergar font whose script does not extract.

entries.english: the three kāyas; the three bodies
entries.notes: ཆོས་སྐུ་ (dharmakāya), ལོངས་སྐུ་ (saṃbhogakāya), སྤྲུལ་སྐུ་ (nirmāṇakāya). སྐུ་ is the honorific for ལུས་ “body”, so the phrase is inherently honorific. Tibetan script reconstructed from the printed phonetics — the Chariot PDF uses a legacy Tergar font whose script does not extract.

example.english: By the blessing of the Buddha, who has attained the three kāyas,

entries.notes: Honorific past stem — the ཞེ་ས་ equivalent of ཐོབ་ “to attain”, used because the subject is the Buddha. Nominalised བརྙེས་པ་ + connective འི་ in v.6i. Tibetan script reconstructed from the printed phonetics — the Chariot PDF uses a legacy Tergar font whose script does not extract.

example.english: By the blessing of the Buddha, who has attained the three kāyas,

entries.english: dharmatā; the nature of phenomena; reality itself
entries.notes: ཆོས་ “phenomenon” + ཉིད་ “-ness”. Parallel in formation to སེམས་ཉིད་ “mind itself”. Here modified by མི་འགྱུར་ “unchanging” — dharmatā is what does not alter. Tibetan script reconstructed from the printed phonetics — the Chariot PDF uses a legacy Tergar font whose script does not extract.

example.english: by the blessing of the unchanging truth of dharmatā,

entries.notes: Negative particle མི་ + present stem འགྱུར་, giving a negated attributive. Note མི་ (not མ་) because the reference is general/atemporal rather than past. Tibetan script reconstructed from the printed phonetics — the Chariot PDF uses a legacy Tergar font whose script does not extract.
sources: Kagyü Ngöndro (Chariot for Traveling the Noble Path)

example.english: by the blessing of the unchanging truth of dharmatā,

entries.notes: Also the noun “half” (ཕྱེད་ཀ་). Negated as མི་ཕྱེད་ “indivisible”. Distinguish from བཅད་ “cut, sever” (NGO1-041) and from ཕྱེ་ “flour; to open”. Tibetan script reconstructed from the printed phonetics — the Chariot PDF uses a legacy Tergar font whose script does not extract.

example.english: and by the blessing of the Saṅgha's indivisible aspiration,

entries.notes: Of the Saṅgha's འདུན་པ་ (aspiration): single and unsplit. Compare དབྱེར་མེད་ and གཉིས་མེད་, which negate divisibility with a noun rather than a verb stem. Tibetan script reconstructed from the printed phonetics — the Chariot PDF uses a legacy Tergar font whose script does not extract.
sources: Kagyü Ngöndro (Chariot for Traveling the Noble Path)

sourceLessons.source: Kagyü Ngöndro (Chariot for Traveling the Noble Path)

example.english: and by the blessing of the Saṅgha's indivisible aspiration,

entries.notes: Direct Sanskrit transliteration, written with the retroflex ཊ ཋ ཌ series used only for loans — hence the unusual ཎ and ྜ. The native Tibetan equivalent is དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་ “centre-and-circumference”. Here it names the seven-heaps/universe offering, not a deity palace.

example.english: The ground anointed with perfumed water and strewn with flowers,

entries.english: the earth; the ground; the earth's surface
entries.notes: ས་ “earth” + གཞི་ “base” — a synonym compound, common in verse where a single syllable would break the metre.

example.english: The ground anointed with perfumed water and strewn with flowers,

entries.notes: IMPORTANT PAIR: homophonous with བཞི་ “four” (NGO1-033) — both ZHI, and both occur in this same four-line verse (ས་གཞི་ in v.a, གླིང་བཞི་ in v.b). Also the “ground” of ground/path/result (གཞི་ ལམ་ འབྲས་བུ་).

example.english: The ground anointed with perfumed water and strewn with flowers,

entries.notes: One of the standard outer offerings. Note that this PDF's font drops the subjoined ྤ, printing སོས་ — read སྤོས་.

example.english: The ground anointed with perfumed water and strewn with flowers,

entries.notes: Distinguish from བཅུ་ “ten” (NGO2-036), a near-pair differing only by the བ prefix.

example.english: The ground anointed with perfumed water and strewn with flowers,

entries.notes: Agentive སྤོས་ཆུས་ in v.a: “with perfumed water”. The published English renders this “with perfume”, folding the water in.

example.english: The ground anointed with perfumed water and strewn with flowers,

entries.notes: Past stem of འབྱུག་པ་ “to anoint, smear, rub on”. Distinguish from འཇུག་པ་ “to enter” (TIB1-078), also JUK — and from ཞུགས་ / བཞུགས་ (ZHUK), which differ in the initial (J vs ZH).

example.english: The ground anointed with perfumed water and strewn with flowers,

entries.notes: IMPORTANT PAIR: ཤིང་ (SHING) vs ཞིང་ (ZHING, NEC-122) are the same ལྷག་བཅས་ particle selected by the preceding final — ཤིང་ after ག ད བ ས, ཞིང་ after ང ན མ ར ལ and no final. Distinguished in Lhasa by the initial (SH vs ZH), and easily confused in writing. The homograph “tree/wood” appears in དཔག་བསམ་ལྗོན་ཤིང་.

example.english: The ground anointed with perfumed water and strewn with flowers,

entries.notes: A standard outer offering. This PDF's font misplaces the vowel, printing མེ་ཏགོ་ — read མེ་ཏོག་. No relation to མེ་ “fire”, despite the spelling.

example.english: The ground anointed with perfumed water and strewn with flowers,

entries.english: strewn; spread out; scattered; displayed (past stem)
entries.notes: Past stem of འགྲེམ་པ་ “to spread out, distribute”. The stem series is highly irregular — worth memorising as a set.

example.english: The ground anointed with perfumed water and strewn with flowers,

entries.english: Mount Meru; the king of mountains
entries.notes: Short for རི་རྒྱལ་ལྷུན་པོ་ / རི་རབ་ལྷུན་པོ་. The cosmological axis at the centre of the four continents — the centrepiece of the maṇḍala offering.

example.english: this, adorned with Mount Meru, the four continents, the sun and moon —

entries.notes: Note the ག prefix + subjoined ླ: read simply LING. Also the “-ling” of monastery names.

example.english: this, adorned with Mount Meru, the four continents, the sun and moon —

entries.notes: The four continents of Abhidharma cosmology surrounding Mount Meru, of which our own is ཛམ་བུ་གླིང་ (Jambudvīpa). Noun before number — the normal Tibetan order.

example.english: this, adorned with Mount Meru, the four continents, the sun and moon —

entries.notes: With ལ་དོན་ དུ་ in v.c: “as a buddha realm”. The ལ་དོན་ marks the role something is imagined *as* — a use worth noting alongside its locative sense.

example.english: by offering [it], having visualized [it] as a buddha realm,

entries.notes: Past stem of འབུལ་བ་ (TIB1-086), the honorific verb of giving — one offers *up*. Nominalised ཕུལ་བ་ + agentive ཡིས་ in v.c: “by offering”.

example.english: by offering [it], having visualized [it] as a buddha realm,

entries.notes: Contraction of བསྔོ་བ་ + སྨོན་ལམ་, used as the section title. Compare the Chariot's full form བསྔོ་བ་སྨོན་ལམ་ (Ngöndro 6) — same pairing, spelled out.

example.english: By this merit, [may all beings], omniscience

entries.english: omniscience; the state of seeing everything
entries.notes: Built on the honorific གཟིགས་པ་ “to see” (TIB1-091) + ཉིད་ “-ness”, so literally “all-seeing-ness”. A synonym of རྣམ་མཁྱེན་ (NEC-107), which builds the same idea on མཁྱེན་པ་ “to know”. The printed page reads correctly; only PDF text-extraction garbles the vowel placement (གཟགི ས་).

example.english: By this merit, [may all beings], omniscience

entries.notes: IMPORTANT PAIR: visually almost identical to དག་ (TIB1-021, plural marker / “pure”) — differing only by the subjoined ྲ, which PDF text-extraction drops (the printed page is correct). Here the enemy is identified as ཉེས་པ་ “wrongdoing” itself.

example.english: having attained, and having defeated the enemies that are wrongdoing,

entries.english: to be defeated; to defeat; defeat
entries.notes: With བྱས་ in ཕམ་བྱས་ “having defeated” — the ཕམ་ + བྱེད་ light-verb pattern makes a transitive from an intransitive root. Contrast རྒྱལ་བ་ “to be victorious” (NEC-106).

example.english: having attained, and having defeated the enemies that are wrongdoing,

entries.english: to age; to grow old; old age
entries.notes: Second member of སྐྱེ་རྒ་ན་འཆི་. Distinguish from དགའ་བ་ “joy” (NEC-011) and རྒན་ “aged, elder” (as in དགེ་རྒན་, མ་རྒན་) — all GA / GEN in Lhasa.

example.english: from the churning waves of birth, ageing, sickness and death,

entries.english: birth, old age, sickness and death
senses: birth, old age, sickness and death
entries.notes: The four sufferings, each a bare verb stem used nominally — a compression only verse allows. Note ན་ here is the verb “to be ill”, not the conditional particle, and འཆི་ takes the connective འི་ before རྦ་རླབས་.

example.english: from the churning waves of birth, ageing, sickness and death,

entries.english: to be turbulent; to be agitated; to churn; turmoil; conflict
entries.notes: Of the waves: churning. Also used of social unrest and of disturbed elements in the body. Distinguish from འཁོར་བ་ “to rotate” and from ཁྲོམ་ “crowd”.

example.english: from the churning waves of birth, ageing, sickness and death,

entries.notes: Systematic opposite of ཐུན་མོང་ “common, shared”: བྱེ་བྲག་ is the particular case, ཐུན་མོང་ the general one. Here བསམ་པ་ “thoughts” and བློ་ཡི་བྱེ་བྲག་ “the distinctions of mind” together name what the teaching is matched to.
